title: Hidden Cracks Help Explain a Mystery on Asteroid Bennu
summary:
When NASA's OSIRIS-REx spacecraft reached the asteroid Bennu in 2018, scientists got a surprise. They expected some smooth, sandy areas. Instead, the surface was covered with huge boulders.

That was puzzling. Earlier measurements from NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope showed that Bennu's surface heats up and cools down quickly as it spins between sunlight and darkness. Scientists call this low thermal inertia. Beach sand behaves this way. Big solid rocks usually do not. Like concrete, they hold heat and release it slowly. So how could a rocky asteroid cool so fast?

OSIRIS-REx collected samples from Bennu and brought them back to Earth. A team led by Andrew Ryan of the University of Arizona studied tiny pieces of the rocks. Their findings were published in the journal Nature Communications.

The team found that the rocks were full of tiny empty spaces. But that alone did not explain the fast cooling. They also discovered that many rock pieces had networks of cracks running through them.

Researchers at Nagoya University in Japan used a laser to heat tiny spots on the samples and watched how the heat spread. The small samples held heat better than the spacecraft had measured on Bennu itself. This suggested that the size of the rocks and their inner structure matter a lot.

At NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, scientists sealed the samples in airtight containers to keep them clean. Then they used 3D X-ray scans, called XCT, to see inside the rocks without harming them. Curator Nicole Lunning compared each container to a spacesuit for the sample.
why_it_matters: Understanding what asteroid rocks are like inside helps scientists read measurements from space correctly and learn how these objects formed and changed.

background_read: Asteroids are rocky leftovers from the time when the planets formed, so studying them can teach scientists about the early solar system.
NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission traveled to the asteroid Bennu, collected pieces of its surface and brought them back to Earth.
Scientists can learn what a surface is made of by measuring how fast it warms in sunlight and cools in darkness.
Returned samples are kept sealed and clean so that Earth's air and water do not change them before they are studied.
